summary: The revision fixes most of what I raised: the Kirin-shaped retainer is gone, red-team access is easier to approve and partners can resell it. But at $6,500 this now costs as much as my whole annual pentest and needs finance approval. I would only pay it with a written customer or auditor request about coding agents in hand, and that trigger is still unproven.

objections.objection: The new price puts the sprint head-to-head with the security spend I already have. $6,500 is about what a small SaaS pays for its whole annual pentest: fixed-price vendors quote $4,000 for web app and API plus $2,400 for cloud, $6,400 in total. That pentest is what customers and SOC 2 auditors actually ask for. At $3,500 I could put it on a card; at $6,500 it needs a budget conversation, and the CFO will ask why a coding-agent test costs as much as the test of our product. Without a written trigger, I defer it to next year's budget.

The must-have trigger is still an assumption, not evidence. The revision narrows the buyer to companies with a written questionnaire item or auditor question about coding agents, but the concept shows none. The enterprise AI questionnaires I can find ask about the vendor's AI product (model behaviour, refusals, retention, training, guardrails), not about how its developers configure Claude Code or MCP. The concept itself says SOC 2 has no AI criteria. The segment that has a real trigger may be very small.

The partner channel may not carry the price through to me. A pentest or vCISO firm buying at $5,000 and adding its margin either charges me more than $6,500 or adds a cheaper 'AI tooling' line to its own scope. Either way, as the buyer I would ask my existing tester for an add-on day, not a separate two-week sprint.

The quarterly re-test costs $7,200 a year, more than the $6,500 sprint. Without a change to our agents or MCP setup I would re-test once a year alongside the pentest, so recurring revenue will be thin.
There is still no money case for the CFO: no avoided-loss figure, no deal value unblocked and no insurer credit. The pitch remains OWASP mappings and findings, which a finance approver discounts.
Bundling erodes the reason to buy again. Vanta, Drata and the agent vendors' managed settings will be good enough for my auditor, so after one sprint I may consider the topic closed.

strongest_point: A fixed-scope, published-price red team with re-test evidence, testing in a disposable environment by default and offering a one-repository entry step is something a CTO can approve quickly once a customer asks.
what_would_change_my_mind: 3 of 10 partner firms show redacted client questionnaires or auditor requests that name coding agents, MCP or CI agent jobs.
At least 1 CTO pays the $1,000 deposit at $6,500 and cites a specific deal or audit as the reason.
A pentest firm sells the sprint at $6,500 or more as a separate line next to its normal pentest rather than folding it into its own scope.
Evidence that the one-repository CI test (priced well under $5,000) converts to the full sprint in at least 1 of 3 cases.

resolved_prior.objection: No must-have trigger; SOC 2 has no AI criteria and questionnaires are covered by an inventory and a policy.
resolved_prior.note: Buyer narrowed to companies with a written trigger and the riskiest assumption now tests it, but no evidence yet that such triggers are common.

resolved_prior.objection: No budget line of its own; I would rather ask my existing pentest or compliance vendor.
resolved_prior.note: Pentest, vCISO and SOC 2 readiness firms are now resellers at wholesale, so the sprint can be their line item. The budget it competes with is still the pentest (see new objection).

resolved_prior.objection: The $400 retainer loses to Knostic Kirin at $15/user/month.
resolved_prior.note: Retainer replaced by a quarterly re-test that Kirin does not do; Kirin recommended for enforcement. The re-test price raises a smaller issue.

resolved_prior.objection: Approval friction for red-teaming production credentials exceeds the price.
resolved_prior.note: Disposable fork, scoped tokens and mock MCP servers by default, a one-repository first step, and paperwork plus insurance planned before launch.

resolved_prior.objection: Hard to justify to a CFO in money terms.
resolved_prior.note: No avoided-loss or deal-unblocked case was added, and this matters more at the higher price.

resolved_prior.objection: Agent vendors bundle managed settings, eroding the reason to pay.
resolved_prior.note: Acknowledged in risks and the core moved to red-teaming, which reduces but does not remove the issue.
